27.0.big: Senses turn things in the world (light, sound, chemicals, pressure) into electrical signals your brain can understand.
points: Special senses have their own organs: smell (olfaction), taste (gustation), hearing, balance, vision. General senses are spread across the body: touch, temperature, pain, and body position (proprioception).

27.1.big: Every sense follows the same steps: reception → transduction → perception.
points: Reception: a sensory receptor detects a specific stimulus. Its receptive field is the area it monitors.

Sensory transduction: the stimulus is turned into an electrical change (a receptor potential), which can trigger action potentials. Some receptors are specialized cells; free nerve endings respond to several kinds of stimuli.
Perception: the brain (cerebral cortex) interprets the signal. Damage to the nerves between receptor and brain blocks perception even if the receptor works.
Just-noticeable difference (JND): the smallest change you can detect. It's proportional to the starting size (Weber's law): you'd notice 1 lb added to a 1 lb bag, but not to a 20 lb bag.

27.2.big: Somatosensation is touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain and body position, all sensed by receptors in the skin, muscles and joints.
points: Mechanoreceptors sense pressure and touch. Near the surface (fine touch): Merkel's discs (light touch; unencapsulated) and Meissner's corpuscles (fine touch and grip). Deeper: Ruffini endings (skin stretch) and Pacinian corpuscles (deep pressure and high-frequency vibration).
Fingertips are packed with Merkel's and Meissner's receptors, which is why they're so sensitive. Smooth, hairless skin is called glabrous. Hair receptors in hairy skin sense hair movement.
Thermoreceptors sense warm and cold. Capsaicin in peppers opens the same calcium channels as heat receptors, so spicy food feels hot.
Nociception = sensing damaging stimuli (pain).
Body position: proprioception (where your limbs are) and kinesthesia (sense of movement), using muscle spindles (muscle stretch) and Golgi tendon organs (tendon tension).

27.3.big: Taste and smell are chemical senses: receptors bind molecules from food or the air.
points: Five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami (savory). Bitter warns of poison and sour warns of spoiled food.
Taste molecules (tastants) bind receptors in taste buds, which sit in bumps called papillae. Each taste cell responds to one type of taste. Filiform papillae have no taste buds.

Smell: odorants bind olfactory receptors in the olfactory epithelium high in the nose. Signals go to the olfactory bulb, where they are sorted in glomeruli. Humans have about 12 million olfactory receptors; dogs have far more (and bigger snouts).
Pheromones are chemical signals between members of the same species. In many animals they go to the amygdala and aren't consciously noticed.

27.4.big: Hearing (audition) and balance (vestibular sense) both use hair cells in the inner ear that bend when fluid moves.
points: Sound is a pressure wave. Pitch = frequency (Hz). Volume = amplitude (decibels). Humans hear about 20–20,000 Hz; bats and dolphins hear far higher (ultrasound).
Outer ear: the auricle (pinna) funnels sound to the tympanum (eardrum). Middle ear: three ossicles — malleus, incus, stapes — amplify vibrations onto the oval window.

Inner ear: the cochlea holds the organ of Corti. Waves move the basilar membrane, bending stereocilia on hair cells against the tectorial membrane. That bending opens ion channels and fires the auditory nerve.
Balance: the labyrinth includes the semicircular canals (head rotation) and the utricle and saccule, where small crystals pulled by gravity sense tilt and straight-line acceleration.

27.5.big: Vision turns light into signals in the retina, and the brain builds them into images.
points: Visible light is a small slice of the spectrum (about 380–700 nm). Shorter wavelength = higher energy (violet/blue). Brightness is measured in candelas.
Path: the cornea bends light, the iris adjusts the pupil, the lens focuses it onto the retina.
Rods: dim light, black and white, use rhodopsin. Cones: color and detail, three types (S, M, L for blue, green, red). The fovea is packed with cones for sharp vision.

Odd twist: light hyperpolarizes rods and cones, which stops their tonic activity (constant neurotransmitter release in the dark). Signals pass to bipolar neurons, then ganglion cells. Some processing happens right in the retina.
Focus problems: myopia (nearsighted; image lands in front of the retina), hyperopia (farsighted; behind it), presbyopia (lens stiffens with age).

In the brain: the superior colliculus coordinates head and eye movement, the suprachiasmatic nucleus sets circadian rhythms from light, and the visual cortex sends "where" information to the parietal lobe and "what" to the temporal lobe.

1.why: Body position (proprioception) is a general sense. The others are special senses.

3.why: Perception happens in the brain's cerebral cortex.

4.why: Turning a stimulus into an electrical signal = transduction.

5.why: The smallest detectable change is the just-noticeable difference.

6.why: Differences under 20% feel the same: a (about 10%), c (about 17%) and d (about 16%) all qualify. Only b (about 21%) is noticeable.

8.why: Merkel's discs are unencapsulated. The others are wrapped in capsules.

10.why: Free nerve endings reach into the epidermis, the outer skin layer.

11.why: Hair receptors are only in hairy skin and sense hairs bending.

13.why: Capsaicin opens the same calcium channels as heat receptors.

15.why: Each taste cell responds to one type of taste.

19.why: Humans have about 12 million olfactory receptors and dogs about a billion: roughly 83 times more.

20.why: The olfactory epithelium fills the snout, so a bigger snout could mean a better nose. That's testable.

21.why: Foliate papillae hold about 1,300 taste buds each.

23.why: Dolphins hear up to 150,000 Hz. Bats top out around 100,000.

26.why: The cochlea holds the receptors that turn vibrations into signals.

27.why: The organ of Corti has hair cells with stereocilia that fire the auditory nerve.

28.why: Hair cells are used in both hearing and balance.

29.why: Gravity pulls the otolith layer sideways, which happens when the head tilts forward.

31.why: Blue has the shortest wavelength of these.

32.why: Light can travel through a vacuum (sound can't).

34.why: Image in front of the retina = myopia (nearsightedness).

35.why: The retina starts processing before signals leave the eye.

36.why: The superior colliculus coordinates head and eye movement.

37.why: Specialized receptors detect one kind of stimulus. Free nerve endings respond to several.

38.why: The receptor still detects and transduces the stimulus, but the signal never reaches the brain, so perception fails.

39.why: The JND drops as sounds get louder (and is lower at higher frequencies), so we notice smaller differences in louder sounds.

40.why: All senses turn a stimulus into an electrical signal carried by the nervous system.

41.why: They're mechanoreceptors for fine detail, which fingertips need more than palms.

42.why: The smallest two-point distances (2.4–2.5 mm) are on the long and little fingers: the most receptors.

43.why: Capsaicin opens the same calcium channels as heat receptors. People differ in how much they can tolerate.

44.why: Merkel's and Meissner's are near the surface (fine touch). Pacinian and Ruffini are deeper (pressure).

45.why: The trend line slopes down: higher BMI, weaker taste on average.

46.why: Without taste it couldn't tell safe from dangerous food (bitter, spoiled, sour or sweet).

47.why: Bloodhounds were bred for more receptors and a bigger olfactory epithelium.

48.why: Pheromones go to the amygdala and aren't consciously noticed.

49.why: Dolphins and whales hear up to about 150 kHz, far above humans' 19 kHz.

51.why: The ossicles carry eardrum vibrations to the stapes and cochlea. Missing a link breaks the chain.

52.why: Balance sensors rely on gravity pulling on crystals, so lower gravity changes how motion feels.

53.why: Warm bodies give off infrared, whose frequency is too low for our eyes.

54.why: White light stimulates all three cones. Rods don't do color (and are saturated in bright light).

55.why: Light hyperpolarizes photoreceptors. Most other receptors depolarize when stimulated.
